You may also indicate whether related outputs are publicly shared, shared with partners or within consortia or not publicly disclosed.
answer:
We have conducted a research project in partnership with Sorbonne University during 24 months to improve accuracy of AI models for scoring and classification, with practical target of imbalance data. We released an open source package, MGS-GRF, and published two papers, in AISTATS and ECML-PKDD, top conferences in machine learning, showcasing how our methods reach unprecedented results on many data-sets and problem of scoring and classification.
We have conducted several research projects to better interpret AI models. We developed a foundation model for retail, that is interpretable and reaches state-of-the-art accuracy. We also developed an open source package, Woodtapper, who has a module that provides an explanation of predictions by the example.
 
We have developed and released an open source package, Woodtapper, that enables to audit any tree-based model, the state of the art of machine learning for tabular data. It was in partnership with Sorbonne University and Societe General, a major French bank, who needs to audit their sensitive use cases. The package enables to explain any model as a simple list of rules, easily interpretable by a human.
 
We have conducted several research projects to measure and improve the fairness of machine learning models. Our package, OT-FairBoost, reaches unprecedented trade-off between accuracy of model and reduced discrimination. We applied it to many scenarios, regression, classification, mitigation of disparate impact or equality of odds. It was conducted in partnership with l’Oréal, University Toulouse 3, and professors affiliated to CNRS and INRIA.

question: What research or investment is your organization pursuing to minimize socio-economic and/or environmental risks from AI?
answer:
Amazon pursues research and investment initiatives aimed at minimizing both socio-economic and environmental risks from AI development and deployment.
 
Amazon is taking a multifaceted approach to balancing AI advancement with environmental and social responsibility. At the infrastructure level, AWS introduced new data center components offering 12% more compute power with improved efficiency, along with direct-to-chip liquid cooling solution for high-density AI compute chips that reduces mechanical energy consumption by up to 46% during peak cooling—without increasing water usage. These improvements helped AWS achieve a global Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of 1.15, compared to the industry average of 1.25.
 
We’re investing in projects to reduce the water footprint of our facilities and expand water availability in the communities where we operate. In 2022, we announced our commitment to being water positive by 2030 returning more water to communities and the environment than we use in AWS data center operations by 1) increasing the use of sustainable water sources, 2) improving water use efficiency across our operations, 3) reusing water as much as possible, and 4) supporting water replenishment projects for communities and the environment around the world. in partnership with the Water Environment Federation, The Water Center at the University of Pennsylvania, and Leading Utilities of the World we established the Water-AI Nexus Center of Excellence. This first-of-its kind initiative leads and convenes research at the intersection of water and AI, advances AI-powered community water solutions and empowers, the next generation of diverse water leaders in the AI era.
 To address the increased energy demands of AI, we focus on optimizing efficiency while scaling carbon-free energy. AI is being used to optimize sizing recommendations to reduce returns, identifying energy inefficiencies, detecting water leaks, and avoiding packaging; solving countless environmental challenges while simultaneously improving service quality. Please see our Amazon Sustainability Report.
 
Through our Clean Energy and Sustainability accelerators, we invest in start-ups, scale-ups, and SMBs driving sustainable innovation. These programs facilitate co-innovation between leading Energy, Utilities & Industrial corporations and clean energy & climate tech innovators. We help entrepreneurs develop their skills and scale their businesses to maximize climate impact, while developing breakthrough technologies to support net-zero goals. In partnership with UNESCO and the International Centre on Artificial Intelligence (IRCAI), our Compute for Climate Fellowship funds proof of concepts climate solutions that leverage advanced cloud computing and generative AI addressing the climate crisis.
 
Additionally, the AWS Imagine Grant program exemplifies our commitment to addressing societal challenges through AI. The program's Pathfinder - Generative AI awards support innovative projects like The Nature Conservancy's development of the first-ever generative AI suite of tools for nature-based science, and RAINN's implementation of AI-powered crisis hotlines for victims of abuse.

question: Please provide a consolidated description of your organisation's approach to risk management across the AI system lifecycle, including how the practices identified above operate together and any cross-cutting governance, review or escalation processes. Please also indicate how often these practices are reviewed and what types of events trigger reviews and updates. Where relevant, please distinguish between different types of AI systems (e.g. generative or agentic AI).
answer: Felaris runs a governance-by-design approach, applied to its own AI work the way it advises clients. At the plan and design stage, a use case is scoped against the EU AI Act risk tiers and the Felaris five-dimension readiness assessment (data, process, people, governance, technology). At the data stage, a data-quality report runs on ingest so gaps are visible before anything is modelled, and per-tenant isolation keeps client data separate. Build and integration use third-party foundation models for extraction, with a human confirmation step on every extracted input. Verification uses a scoped pilot on one decision and one data domain, tested against a recent event the organisation already lived through. Deployment is gated by dev/production separation, data residency, and sign-off against the Felaris AI Governance framework. Operation is designed for model and data drift monitoring, a use register and an incident register with named owners, and a quarterly review. Practices are reviewed at each release and on any incident. Felaris does not build agentic AI, and its applications are pre-production.

question: If yes, please describe key research or investment initiatives in the areas selected above (e.g., dedicated safety teams, funding of research programs, contributions to open-source safety tools, publishing research, partnerships and collaborative research initiatives). You may also indicate whether related outputs are publicly shared, shared with partners or within consortia or not publicly disclosed.
answer:
Fujitsu is advancing research, development, implementation, and external collaboration on both AI ethics governance and AI trust technology to realize the social implementation of safe, secure, and reliable AI.
In terms of AI ethics governance, Fujitsu formulated and published the "Fujitsu Group AI Commitment" in 2019, outlining its policy to prioritize value creation through AI, human-centricity, sustainability, respect for human decision-making, transparency, and accountability. They have also established an external AI Ethics Committee, incorporating insights from outside experts in diverse fields such as law, biomedical science, SDGs, and consumer administration, not just AI. Furthermore, the AI Ethics Office leads the Fujitsu Group's AI ethics governance strategy, internal practices, and external dissemination, conducting comprehensive ethical risk reviews for all AI businesses and providing AI ethics education for all employees. 
Regarding research and development, Fujitsu is promoting R&D in AI ethics technology based on four pillars: compliance with laws and guidelines, Ethics-by-Design and AI governance, addressing biases inherent in generative AI, and tackling social issues. Specifically, they offer and make public tools such as AI Ethics Impact Assessment to identify and evaluate ethical risks before designing AI services, Fujitsu AI Ethics for Fairness to verify and improve the fairness of AI training data and decisions (including intersectional fairness), Fujitsu LLM Bias Diagnosis to identify bias in LLMs, and AI Risk Management Tools to manage ethical, quality, and security risks inherent in each phase of the AI lifecycle. 
In the security aspect of generative AI and advanced AI systems, Fujitsu has developed a "LLM Vulnerability Scanner & Guardrails" that comprehensively evaluates LLM vulnerabilities and automatically applies optimal defense technologies to generative AI. This technology aims to enable even non-experts to safely operate generative AI, addressing the challenges of increasing attacks on generative AI, diversifying attack methods, and a shortage of experts.
For further technical details:
LLM Vulnerability Scanner & Guardrails (Fujitsu Research)
Additionally, in multi-AI agent security technology, Fujitsu is advancing R&D to support proactive measures against new threats to IT systems and generative AI by linking attacking AI agents, defending AI agents, and testing AI agents. 
To address misinformation and disinformation and social risks, in response to the societal problem of misinformation and disinformation circulation caused by generative AI and synthetic content, Fujitsu has embarked on technology development for misinformation and disinformation analysis as part of a NEDO public solicitation project under the "Economic Security Important Technology Development Program" in collaboration with the Cabinet Office and the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. This initiative is advancing R&D for a misinformation and disinformation countermeasure system that combines misinformation and disinformation detection for each medium, evidence and endorsement management, comprehensive truthfulness judgment support, and misinformation and disinformation impact assessment.
Furthermore, Fujitsu is working on building a misinformation and disinformation countermeasure platform in an "All-Japan" framework involving nine industry-academia partners, which integrates processes from misinformation and disinformation detection to evidence gathering, analysis, and evaluation. In addition, Fujitsu has founded "Frontria", an international consortium to address misinformation and disinformation and new AI risks, bringing together cutting-edge technologies and knowledge from around the world to create a digital society that combines trust and safety.
Through these efforts, Fujitsu continuously promotes R&D to enhance the safety, security, fairness, explainability, transparency, robustness, and trustworthiness of AI, linking research outcomes to AI services, AI platforms, and social implementation.

question: Describe key privacy measures and data-protection standards applied.
answer:
We have established and published the “NEC Privacy Policy,” which complies with the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and “JIS Q 15001: Personal Information Protection Management Systems—Requirements,” and we have implemented management systems and technical measures throughout our entire group, both in Japan and overseas.
1. Basic Policy, Applicable Standards, and Company-wide Implementation Framework
We obtained Privacy Mark certification in October 2005 and have been continuously maintaining and renewing it (we completed our ninth certification renewal in October 2021).
We designate a person responsible for managing personal information in each department that handles personal information, take measures to ensure that personal information is not handled beyond the scope necessary to achieve the specified purposes of use, and strive to prevent leaks, loss, and damage through necessary and appropriate security measures.
Based on our cybersecurity checklist, we protect privacy and data throughout the entire development lifecycle of our products, systems, and services. Key measures include identifying and assessing risks to protected assets such as personal information, trade secrets, and authentication credentials; clarifying the division of responsibilities with customers and defining SLAs; implementing access control based on the principle of least privilege; encrypting stored data, backups, and communication channels; ensuring secure cryptographic key management; preventing the output of confidential information in logs and applying masking; restricting the use of confidential information in test data; monitoring access during operations; deleting unnecessary accounts and access rights; and performing irreversible data erasure when disposing of media. This checklist incorporates the principles of ISO/IEC 15408 and draws on the privacy and security management measures outlined in NIST SP 800-53.
We also require third parties with whom we share or outsource data to comply with security measures equivalent to those of our Group.
 2. Technical Safety Management Measures
We implement access control based on identification and authentication, measures to prevent unauthorized external access, and encryption during transmission (such as TLS), tailored to the risks associated with each operational phase.
We prevent information leaks in the event of theft, loss, or accidental transmission by applying storage device and file encryption (encryption at rest) as the default security level across the entire NEC Group and by appropriately configuring access rights and usage expiration dates.
To meet customers’ security requirements and data sovereignty demands, we offer multiple deployment options—including on-premises, the domestically developed and operated cloud “NEC Cloud Storage (St)” (limited to domestic data centers), and hybrid models—providing choices that help avoid the risks associated with the cross-border transfer of highly confidential data.
We provide a filtering function for sensitive information and personal information when entering prompts into generative AI systems, and have established a mechanism that allows users to proactively protect their data according to their risk level.
3. Privacy-Enhancing Technologies (PETs) and Advanced Research and Development
We are conducting research and development on “highly secure federated learning,” which combines federated learning—a technique that utilizes training data from various organizations in a distributed manner rather than aggregating it in a single location—with secure computation, which enables computational processing while the data remains encrypted. We are advancing research on this technology to prevent the inference of training data from model parameters while also avoiding a decline in AI accuracy.
At our lab, we are conducting research on a technology that combines differential privacy with federated learning to provide a theoretical guarantee that training data cannot be inferred from model outputs.
We are working on synthetic data generation technology that can be used for training and validating AI models without using real data (creating synthetic data that reproduces statistical characteristics using generative AI).
We are conducting research and development on technologies that enable training without disclosing confidential data during additional training (fine-tuning), and have successfully demonstrated the ability to run “cotomi” for inference in a confidential computing environment.

question: Does your organization collaborate with civil society and community groups to identify and develop AI solutions in support of the UN Sustainable Development Goals and to address the world's greatest challenges? Please provide examples.
answer:
OpenAI’s UN General Assembly (UNGA) activation in 2024 brought together global governments, civil society, and our nonprofit partners (Kytabu, Digital Green, Visao Coop, and 10bedicu.org) to discuss progress toward addressing the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Our CEO Sam Altman launched our OpenAI Academy program at UNGA to support global organizations advancing development and hosted fireside chats with the UN Deputy Secretary General and the UN Tech Envoy on addressing the world’s pressing challenges with AI. At UNGA we also brought together representatives from USAID, UNICEF, UNDP, UNESCO, the Center for Global Development, International Rescue Committee, along with the governments of Togo, Nigeria, and Iceland, and our nonprofit partners to discuss the importance of preserving low-resource languages and the power of AI tools to help people solve hard problems being addressed by the UN.
While we may be the ones building the technology, the real-world applications are emerging from the ingenuity of our users. The initiatives below demonstrates AI's groundbreaking potential:
In India the World Bank estimates that there are 0.7 physicians and 1.7 nurses for every 1,000 people. 10BedICU (https://10bedicu.org/) is addressing this shortage by developing a number of GPT-4 powered tools, including an automated discharge summary generator, that frees up medical providers’ time to focus on patient care. They are also using GPT-4 Vision to sync outdated monitors with their digital EMR system, increasing the accuracy of patient records.
Digital Green (https://digitalgreen.org/) is addressing the shortage of agricultural extension workers with Farmer.Chat (https://farmerchat.digitalgreen.org/), an AI assistant that delivers agricultural expertise tailored to a specific community and context. Digital Green is working with India’s Ministry of Agriculture to deploy Farmer.Chat across 12 Indian states. This will enable extension workers to reach farmers with more relevant advice, ultimately increasing farmer income.
In Kenya, Kytabu (https://kytabu.africa/) is currently using GPT-4 to pilot Somanasi (https://kytabu.africa/somanasi/), a supplementary learning app integrated with the Kenyan curriculum that helps students reinforce classroom learning at their own pace with engaging, gamified tools. This is particularly helpful for students with learning disabilities, who can dig deeper into classroom content without fear of embarrassment. Somanasi is currently being tested in ten schools, with plans to eventually make it accessible to all 33,000 (https://www.education.go.ke/) primary and secondary schools in Kenya.
In Sierra Leone and Ghana, Rising Academies (https://www.risingacademies.com/) has built Rori (https://rori.ai/), a WhatsApp-based math tutor designed to support distance learning. Rori helps low-literacy, low-income students build their foundational math skills by making learning fun.
These initiatives are a small sample of the myriad of ways we are seeing people around the world deploy our technology to improve lives in their communities. The experts who develop these applications to meet local needs are integral to our efforts to build these technologies in ways that can benefit everyone.
OpenAI is also directly investing in innovative AI-powered solutions in service of the SDGs through its AI for Global Development accelerator program, in partnership with the Center for Global Development and the Agency Fund. We are providing technical advisory, cash funding, and API credits to eight nonprofits working in education, health, and agriculture across India, Kenya, South Africa, Botswana, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Ethiopia. These include Rocket Learning, which provides personalized learning pathways for parents and daycare workers to provide early childhood education in India; Noora Health, which equips caregivers with knowledge to support the health of family members in India; and Jacaranda Health, which offers personalized prenatal health advice in local languages in Kenya.
 
We recognize that there is still significant work to be done to develop AI ecosystems that foster broadly distributed benefits of these technologies in the long-term. Significant resourcing will be needed to strengthen AI ecosystems, such as deepening low-resource language datasets, researching and adapting to potential workforce impacts, and rapidly expanding AI literacy.
